newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal's telecom sector remains attractive - analysis.
newsitem.headline: Portugal's telecom sector remains attractive - analysis.

text.p: Despite recent sharp stock price gains, analysts say Portugal's telecommunications sector remains an attractive prospect, probably outshining even that of Spain and Italy.

Together with the good outlook for growth for Portugal Telecom and mobile phone group Telecel goes the advantage of having two extra years in which to prepare for the liberalisation of the European telecommunications market, they said.
"Portugal Telecom has a big advantage over Telefonica because in just 11 months, the Spanish market is going to be open (to competition)," said analyst Jose Freire of Espirito Santo Research.
Portugal has until January 1, 2000, to end restrictions to competition under an accord with the European Union.

"The fundamentals are pretty good, both for Portugal Telecom (PT) and for Telecel. The market is looking for significant growth in their results in 1997 and 1998, above that of main foreign rivals," said analyst Joao Vermelho of Central Investimentos.

Analysts forecast that Portugal Telecom, whose stock price has risen over 20 percent this year to 5,416 escudos, will post a net profit above 60 billion escudos, compared with forecasts for net profit of above 50 billion in 1996.
Telecel's profits should surge from over seven billion escudos last year to 10 billion in 1997, against just 2.4 billion in 1995, they add.

"The room for growth for both PT and Telecel is still very big. The level of market penetration in both mobile and fixed lines is lower than for other European competitors," said Jose Antonio Goncalves of brokers Tottadealer.
Analysts said that it was normal for foreign investors in particular to bundle the southern European telecommunications companies together when weighing an investment.
"Every time that one of them starts to attract interest, the others also tend to benefit," said Freire.
Another element helping Portugal Telecom was the fact that from 1998 onwards, it could stop making provisions against its pension exposure arising from programmed layoffs.

"The plan for cutting staff -- around 3,000-3,200 workers -- ends in 1997. This means that contributions for the pension fund are going to fall significantly, perhaps by 20 billion escudos between 1997 and 1998," said Freire.

Analysts said that the rise in Portugal Telecom's operating margins would allow it to press ahead with the restructuring of its charges, cutting long distance and international calls and boosting local charges.
